The reproductive biology of Red lionfish begins with the release of gametes during broadcast spawning, a strategy common among scorpaenids. Following external fertilisation, the resulting transparent, pelagic eggs develop rapidly. At a constant water temperature of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C], the incubation period is quite brief; hatching, or eclosion, occurs after approximately 3.5 days [ab = approximately 3.5 days]. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva, or prolarva, is lecithotrophic and depends entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves. At this initial stage, the wet weight at birth is exceptionally low, calculated at just 0.00027 grams [Wwb = just 0.00027 grams] based on an egg diameter of 0.8 millimeters. This minuscule mass reflects the tiny size of the fertilised ovum and is typical of pelagic-spawning teleosts that produce large numbers of small offspring. The duration of this yolk-dependent, non-feeding phase is critical; the larva must complete yolk absorption and initiate first exogenous feeding before reaching the point of no reserve. The rapid pace of early development at this temperature is a key determinant of larval survival in the planktonic environment.

As the yolk-sac larva transitions to exogenous feeding, the pelagic larval phase begins. During this period, the free-swimming larva grows and undergoes significant morphological changes. For female Red lionfish, the total length at which puberty is attained is 16 centimeters [Lp = 16 centimeters]. This length marks the onset of gonad maturation and the commencement of vitellogenesis. At this point of sexual maturation, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is calculated to be approximately 41.57 grams [Wwp = approximately 41.57 grams]. This relationship between length and mass indicates a robust body condition at the time of reproductive activation. The transition from a planktivorous juvenile to a reproductively viable organism involves a substantial investment in somatic growth. The ability to reach this size threshold is dependent on prey availability and habitat quality on the reef. Individuals that grow more slowly may experience a delay in the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis, thus postponing their first spawning event.

Upon reaching full sexual maturation, adult Red lionfish can attain a considerable size. The ultimate total length reported for this species reaches 45.7 centimeters [Li = 45.7 centimeters], a value recorded from large, presumably old individuals. Associated with this maximum length, the ultimate wet weight is estimated to be around 1050 grams [Wwi = around 1050 grams], derived from length-weight relationships established for the species. This asymptotic mass represents the upper limit of somatic growth. As iteroparous adults, individuals are capable of spawning multiple times throughout their lives. The maximum lifespan recorded for Pterois volitans, when maintained at 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C], is approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years]. This longevity is relatively extended for a tropical reef fish and allows for many reproductive seasons. The combination of a long life and repeated spawning events contributes to the species' high invasive potential outside its native Pacific range.

The timing of early life stages is tightly coupled with thermal conditions. At a stable temperature of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C], the age at birth is approximately 3.5 days [ab = approximately 3.5 days], a period that is surprisingly short for a fish that hatches as an undeveloped larva. The chorion rupture and emergence of the yolk-sac fry occur rapidly after gamete fusion. This rapid hatching is an adaptation to the high predation pressure in the planktonic environment. The prolarva, still carrying a substantial yolk sac, must quickly develop the mouth gape necessary for first prey capture. The switch from endogenous to exogenous nutrition is a critical bottleneck. The brief egg stage, combined with the small size of the newly hatched larva, underscores the trade-off between fecundity and per-offspring investment. This life-history strategy, characterized by high fecundity and minimal parental care, is a hallmark of many invasive species and explains the lionfish's ability to rapidly colonize new habitats.

The extensive longevity of Pterois volitans has significant implications for population dynamics. Field records indicate that the maximum recorded longevity in the wild can reach a full decade (10 years) [am = 10 years] under optimal conditions at 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C]. This lifespan completion is notable among scorpaenids, many of which have shorter lives. The senescent adult death that eventually occurs is typically due to predation or age-related physiological decline rather than a single, programmed post-spawning death. Over this long life, a female will spawn repeatedly, producing multiple clutches. The total length at puberty for females is 16 centimeters [Lp = 16 centimeters], a threshold that is reached within the first year or two of life under favorable conditions. The combination of early maturation and a long reproductive lifespan allows for a high lifetime reproductive output, a factor that complicates management efforts in invaded ecosystems such as the Caribbean and Gulf of Mexico. Understanding these life-history parameters is essential for developing effective control strategies.
